claim: METTL3 and METTL14 complex transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to N6 amino group of adenosine bases in RNA (m6A).
source: Methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 complex transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to N6 amino group of adenosine bases in RNA (m6A) and DNA (m6dA).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of the METTL3-METTL14 complex.

claim: METTL3 and METTL14 complex transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to N6 amino group of adenosine bases in DNA (m6dA).
source: Methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 complex transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to N6 amino group of adenosine bases in RNA (m6A) and DNA (m6dA).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of the METTL3-METTL14 complex.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 preferentially catalyzes the formation of m6dA in single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).
source: we uncover an inverse relationship for substrate binding and methylation and show that METTL3-METTL14 preferentially catalyzes the formation of m6dA in single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), despite weaker binding affinity to DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from methyltransferase assays and binding studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 has weaker binding affinity to DNA compared to RNA.
source: we uncover an inverse relationship for substrate binding and methylation and show that METTL3-METTL14 preferentially catalyzes the formation of m6dA in single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), despite weaker binding affinity to DNA.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assays showing higher Kd values for DNA substrates.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 binds structured RNAs with high affinity.
source: In contrast, it binds structured RNAs with high affinity, but methylates the target adenosine in RNA (m6A) much less efficiently than it does in ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data showing low Kd values (2-25 nM) for structured RNAs like rNEAT2 and rTCE23.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 methylates the target adenosine in RNA (m6A) much less efficiently than it does in ssDNA.
source: In contrast, it binds structured RNAs with high affinity, but methylates the target adenosine in RNA (m6A) much less efficiently than it does in ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assays and mass spectrometry data comparing methylation efficiency on RNA versus DNA substrates.

claim: METTL3-METTL14-mediated methylation of DNA is largely restricted by structured RNA elements prevalent in long noncoding and other cellular RNAs.
source: We also show that METTL3-METTL14-mediated methylation of DNA is largely restricted by structured RNA elements prevalent in long noncoding and other cellular RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent inhibition of DNA methylation by structured RNAs.

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is considered a major covalent modification of the adenosine (A) base in coding and noncoding (nc) RNAs.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is considered a major covalent modification of the adenosine (A) base in coding and noncoding (nc) RNAs (Desrosiers et al., 1974; Bokar et al., 1994; Rottman et al., 1994; Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: m6A is linked to RNA turnover.
source: It is linked to diverse physiological processes, including – but not limited to – RNA turnover (Ke et al., 2017; Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), stem cell differentiation (Batista et al., 2014; Geula et al., 2015,) oncogenic translation (Lin et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017; Choe et al., 2018), and DNA damage repair (Xiang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: m6A is linked to stem cell differentiation.
source: It is linked to diverse physiological processes, including – but not limited to – RNA turnover (Ke et al., 2017; Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), stem cell differentiation (Batista et al., 2014; Geula et al., 2015,) oncogenic translation (Lin et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017; Choe et al., 2018), and DNA damage repair (Xiang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: m6A is linked to oncogenic translation.
source: It is linked to diverse physiological processes, including – but not limited to – RNA turnover (Ke et al., 2017; Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), stem cell differentiation (Batista et al., 2014; Geula et al., 2015,) oncogenic translation (Lin et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017; Choe et al., 2018), and DNA damage repair (Xiang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: m6A is linked to DNA damage repair.
source: It is linked to diverse physiological processes, including – but not limited to – RNA turnover (Ke et al., 2017; Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), stem cell differentiation (Batista et al., 2014; Geula et al., 2015,) oncogenic translation (Lin et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017; Choe et al., 2018), and DNA damage repair (Xiang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most m6A in cellular RNAs is installed by methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 methyltransferases in human cells.
source: In human cells, most m6A in cellular RNAs is installed by methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 methyltransferases (Bokar et al., 1994; Dominissini et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014), both of which belong to the β-class of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (N6-MTases) (Bujnicki et al., 2002; Woodcock et al., 2020) that also include N6-deoxyadenosine DNA methyltransferases (m6dA MTases), especially those from Type III restriction-modification (R-M) systems in bacteria (e.g., ModA/B dimer of EcoP15I) (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: METTL3 and METTL14 belong to the β-class of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (N6-MTases).
source: In human cells, most m6A in cellular RNAs is installed by methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 methyltransferases (Bokar et al., 1994; Dominissini et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014), both of which belong to the β-class of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (N6-MTases) (Bujnicki et al., 2002; Woodcock et al., 2020) that also include N6-deoxyadenosine DNA methyltransferases (m6dA MTases), especially those from Type III restriction-modification (R-M) systems in bacteria (e.g., ModA/B dimer of EcoP15I) (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The β-class of SAM-dependent methyltransferases includes N6-deoxyadenosine DNA methyltransferases (m6dA MTases) from Type III restriction-modification systems in bacteria.
source: In human cells, most m6A in cellular RNAs is installed by methyltransferase like-3 (METTL3) and METTL14 methyltransferases (Bokar et al., 1994; Dominissini et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014), both of which belong to the β-class of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (N6-MTases) (Bujnicki et al., 2002; Woodcock et al., 2020) that also include N6-deoxyadenosine DNA methyltransferases (m6dA MTases), especially those from Type III restriction-modification (R-M) systems in bacteria (e.g., ModA/B dimer of EcoP15I) (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The first structures of METTL3-METTL14 complexes suggested common features in EcoP15I and METTL3-METTL14.
source: The first structures of METTL3-METTL14 complexes suggested common features in EcoP15I and METTL3-METTL14 (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: There is high structural similarity of the cores of human METTL3, METTL14, and EcoP15I.
source: We analyzed these MTases and found high structural similarity of the cores of human METTL3, METTL14, and EcoP15I, suggesting their evolutionary origin from a common ancestor (Figure 1a–e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison shown in Figure 1.

claim: METTL3, METTL14, and EcoP15I share an evolutionary origin from a common ancestor.
source: We analyzed these MTases and found high structural similarity of the cores of human METTL3, METTL14, and EcoP15I, suggesting their evolutionary origin from a common ancestor (Figure 1a–e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity observed in the analysis.

claim: All three members (EcoP15I Mod, METTL3, and METTL14) belong to the β-class of SAM-dependent MTases and exhibit a sequential arrangement of motifs (IV-X followed by motif I).
source: All three members belong to the β-class of SAM-dependent MTases and exhibit a sequential arrangement of motifs (IV-X followed by motif I) (Bujnicki et al., 2002; Woodcock et al., 2020; Malone et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and supported by citations.

claim: Motif IV (D/EPPY/W/L) is associated with the recognition of target adenine base.
source: Motif IV (D/EPPY/W/L) and I are associated with the recognition of target adenine base (Gupta et al., 2015) and co-factor (SAM) binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016a), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and supported by a citation.

claim: Motif I is associated with co-factor (SAM) binding.
source: Motif IV (D/EPPY/W/L) and I are associated with the recognition of target adenine base (Gupta et al., 2015) and co-factor (SAM) binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016a), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and supported by citations.

claim: An overlay of MTase domains of EcoP15I and METTL14 shows structural similarity within MTase folds (rmsd = 2.55 Å over 278 Cα atoms).
source: An overlay of MTase domains of EcoP15I and METTL14 (PDB ID: 5IL0) shows structural similarity within MTase folds (rmsd = 2.55 Å over 278 Cα atoms).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison result shown in Figure 1e.

claim: m6dA in bacterial DNA is deposited in a strictly sequence-dependent manner in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).
source: While m6dA in bacterial DNA is deposited in a strictly sequence-dependent manner in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (Gupta et al., 2015; Malone et al., 1995), m6A in RNA by human METTL3-METTL14 shows less stringent sequence dependency for sequences flanking the target A within the recognition motif DRACH (D = A/G/U, R = A/G, H = A/C/U) (Bokar et al., 1994; Liu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: m6A in RNA by human METTL3-METTL14 shows less stringent sequence dependency for sequences flanking the target A within the recognition motif DRACH.
source: While m6dA in bacterial DNA is deposited in a strictly sequence-dependent manner in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (Gupta et al., 2015; Malone et al., 1995), m6A in RNA by human METTL3-METTL14 shows less stringent sequence dependency for sequences flanking the target A within the recognition motif DRACH (D = A/G/U, R = A/G, H = A/C/U) (Bokar et al., 1994; Liu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: m6A levels in cellular RNA remain at ~0.1% of total pool of ribonucleotides in cultured mammalian cells.
source: However, this does not correlate with low levels of m6A in cellular RNA, which remains at ~0.1% of total pool of ribonucleotides in cultured mammalian cells (Dubin and Taylor, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All m6A is deposited co-transcriptionally, with most occurring on chromatin-associated RNAs.
source: Of note, recent evidence suggests that all m6A is deposited co-transcriptionally, with most occurring on chromatin-associated RNAs, for example, nascent pre-mRNA (CA-RNA), promoter-associated RNA, enhancer RNA, and repeat RNA elements (Ke et al., 2017; Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Slobodin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The METTL3-METTL14 m6A writers can be recruited to chromatin by modified histone tails (e.g., H3K36me3).
source: Consistently, the METTL3-METTL14 m6A writers can be recruited to chromatin by modified histone tails (e.g., H3K36me3) (Huang et al., 2019b) or the transcription machinery (Barbieri et al., 2017; Slobodin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The METTL3-METTL14 m6A writers can be recruited to chromatin by the transcription machinery.
source: Consistently, the METTL3-METTL14 m6A writers can be recruited to chromatin by modified histone tails (e.g., H3K36me3) (Huang et al., 2019b) or the transcription machinery (Barbieri et al., 2017; Slobodin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chromatin-associated XIST lncRNA harbors m6A marks.
source: Certain long noncoding (lnc) RNAs that are essential for regulated transcription, such as chromatin-associated XIST (Patil et al., 2016) and NEAT2 (MALAT1) (Liu et al., 2015), also harbor m6A marks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NEAT2 (MALAT1) lncRNA harbors m6A marks.
source: Certain long noncoding (lnc) RNAs that are essential for regulated transcription, such as chromatin-associated XIST (Patil et al., 2016) and NEAT2 (MALAT1) (Liu et al., 2015), also harbor m6A marks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A role of m6A in DNA damage response and repair has been suggested.
source: A role of m6A in DNA damage response and repair has also been suggested (Zhang et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: METTL3 localizes at sites of dsDNA breaks and installs the m6A on DNA-damage-associated RNAs.
source: In those contexts, METTL3 localizes at sites of dsDNA breaks and installs the m6A on DNA-damage-associated RNAs (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: METTL3 is a pro-viral host factor in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis.
source: METTL3 is also emerged as a pro-viral host factor in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as an emerging finding.

claim: Genetic depletion or inhibition of METTL3 by small molecules triggers innate immune response and limits viral growth.
source: Consistently, genetic depletion or inhibition of METTL3 by small molecules triggers innate immune response and limits viral growth (Burgess et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 can convert dA to m6dA within equivalent DRACH motif in a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with a 2.5-fold preference over the equivalent RNA in vitro.
source: A recent study showed that METTL3-METTL14 can convert dA to m6dA within equivalent DRACH (D = A/G/U, R = A/G, H = A/C/U) motif in a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with a 2.5-fold preference over the equivalent RNA in vitro (Woodcock et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: m6dA levels in mammalian DNA are extremely low (0.006–0.01%).
source: Since m6dA levels in mammalian DNA are extremely low (0.006–0.01%) and thought to originate from RNA catabolism rather than from SAM-dependent MTase reactions (Musheev et al., 2020), fundamental questions about substrate(s) specificity and mechanisms of action of METTL3-METTL14 have emerged.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: m6dA in mammalian DNA is thought to originate from RNA catabolism rather than from SAM-dependent MTase reactions.
source: Since m6dA levels in mammalian DNA are extremely low (0.006–0.01%) and thought to originate from RNA catabolism rather than from SAM-dependent MTase reactions (Musheev et al., 2020), fundamental questions about substrate(s) specificity and mechanisms of action of METTL3-METTL14 have emerged.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A secondary structure-based superposition of EcoP15I ModB and METTL14 revealed common features and similar arrangement of canonical MTase motifs.
source: We compared the MTase cores of (ModB) of EcoP15I (aa 90–132, 169–261, 385–511, PDB: 4ZCF Gupta et al., 2015) and METTL14 (aa 116–402, PDB: 5IL0 Wang et al., 2016b). A secondary structure-based superposition (Krissinel and Henrick, 2004) of these two structures revealed common features and similar arrangement of canonical MTase motifs (motifs I and IV-X), including the motif IV (D/EPPY/W/L) that surrounds the Watson-Crick edge of the flipped target adenine base (Figure 1a–e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison.

claim: Three loops encompassing the sequence intervening MTase motifs IV and V (loop 1), VIII and VIII' (loop 2), and motifs IX and X (loop 3) contribute to substrate binding.
source: Previous studies identified three loops encompassing the sequence intervening MTase motifs IV and V (loop 1), VIII and VIII' (loop 2), and motifs IX and X (loop 3) contribute to substrate binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The MTase domain of METTL14 is enzymatically inactive.
source: While the MTase domain of METTL14 is enzymatically inactive, it harbors features that contribute to substrate binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The MTase domain of METTL14 harbors features that contribute to substrate binding.
source: While the MTase domain of METTL14 is enzymatically inactive, it harbors features that contribute to substrate binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Sledz and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 exhibited higher enzymatic activity on the d6T DNA oligo compared with its RNA counterpart (r6T).
source: We observed higher enzymatic activity of METTL3-METTL14 on the d6T DNA oligo compared with its RNA counterpart (r6T) (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2a and c.

claim: The 14-mer d6T/r6T oligos have a propensity to form duplex DNA (for d6T) or RNA (for r6T).
source: By closely examining the sequence of the 14-mer d6T/r6T, we found a propensity of these oligos to form duplex DNA (for d6T) or RNA (for r6T): 6 of the 14 nucleotides at 5'-end will pair with a complementary sequence to create a duplex with an 8-nt overhang at the 3'-end of each strand (Figures 1g and 2d).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and predicted secondary structures.

claim: The methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 toward d6T* increased by 2-fold compared with d6T.
source: Indeed, we found that the methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 toward d6T* increased by 2-fold compared with d6T (and >12-fold compared with r6T) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 toward d6T* increased by >12-fold compared with r6T.
source: Indeed, we found that the methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 toward d6T* increased by 2-fold compared with d6T (and >12-fold compared with r6T) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 showed no activity in the presence of a perfect duplex version of d6T DNA (d6T-ds).
source: Consistent with previous observations (Woodcock et al., 2019), METTL3-METTL14 showed no activity in the presence of a perfect duplex version of d6T DNA (d6T-ds).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and consistent with previous research.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 showed some low but consistently detectable methyltransferase activity on rNEAT2.
source: We observed no methyltransferase activity on rTCE23 RNA, as expected; but surprisingly, some low (but consistently detectable) methyltransferase activity on rNEAT2 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: METTL3-METTL14 showed no methyltransferase activity on rTCE23 RNA.
source: We observed no methyltransferase activity on rTCE23 RNA, as expected; but surprisingly, some low (but consistently detectable) methyltransferase activity on rNEAT2 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM).
source: The full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM), followed by the hairpin rTCE23 (Kd = 25 nM), the 3'-overhang r6T (Kd = 114 nM), the palindromic Pal-Top+ bot (Kd = 127 nM), and the ssRNA FoxM1-p1 (Kd = 294 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rTCE23 with Kd = 25 nM.
source: The full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM), followed by the hairpin rTCE23 (Kd = 25 nM), the 3'-overhang r6T (Kd = 114 nM), the palindromic Pal-Top+ bot (Kd = 127 nM), and the ssRNA FoxM1-p1 (Kd = 294 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to r6T with Kd = 114 nM.
source: The full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM), followed by the hairpin rTCE23 (Kd = 25 nM), the 3'-overhang r6T (Kd = 114 nM), the palindromic Pal-Top+ bot (Kd = 127 nM), and the ssRNA FoxM1-p1 (Kd = 294 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to Pal-Top+ bot with Kd = 127 nM.
source: The full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM), followed by the hairpin rTCE23 (Kd = 25 nM), the 3'-overhang r6T (Kd = 114 nM), the palindromic Pal-Top+ bot (Kd = 127 nM), and the ssRNA FoxM1-p1 (Kd = 294 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to FoxM1-p1 with Kd = 294 nM.
source: The full-length METTL3-METTL14 binds to rNEAT2 with the highest affinity (Kd = 2 nM), followed by the hairpin rTCE23 (Kd = 25 nM), the 3'-overhang r6T (Kd = 114 nM), the palindromic Pal-Top+ bot (Kd = 127 nM), and the ssRNA FoxM1-p1 (Kd = 294 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: DNA substrates (d6T and d6T*) that showed highest methyltransferase activity were the poorest binders, with Kd values of 370 and 509 nM, respectively.
source: Surprisingly, the DNA substrates (d6T and d6T*) that showed highest methyltransferase activity were the poorest binders, with Kd values of 370 and 509 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between substrate binding affinity and methylation activity for METTL3-METTL14.
source: Surprisingly, the DNA substrates (d6T and d6T*) that showed highest methyltransferase activity were the poorest binders, with Kd values of 370 and 509 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of binding and methylation data across multiple substrates.

claim: The methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 was significantly reduced in the presence of RNA.
source: The methyltransferase activity of METTL3-METTL14 was significantly reduced in the presence of RNA (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: RNAs with propensity to form secondary structures and highest binding affinity to METTL3-METTL14 (rNEAT2, rTCE23) attenuated methyltransferase activity to the most negligible levels.
source: Of note, RNAs with propensity to form secondary structures and highest binding affinity to METTL3-METTL14 (rNEAT2, rTCE23) attenuated methyltransferase activity to the most negligible levels (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Higher methylation levels were observed for rNEAT2* compared to rNEAT2, most likely attributed to a perfect GGACU motif in rNEAT2*.
source: Although higher methylation levels were observed for rNEAT2* compared to rNEAT2, most likely attributed to a perfect GGACU motif in rNEAT2*, yet the methylation was significantly lower than that of d6T* DNA (last panel of Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: rNEAT2* showed ~6 fold reduction in affinity compared to rNEAT2.
source: Moreover, rNEAT2* showed ~6 fold reduction in affinity compared to rNEAT2 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: rNEAT2* attenuated methylation of the single-stranded d6T* DNA by METTL3-METL14 but to a lesser extent than the rNEAT2.
source: Importantly, rNEAT2* also attenuated methylation of the single-stranded d6T* DNA by METTL3-METL14 but to a lesser extent than the rNEAT2 (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by radiometric assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The sequence and shape of the target RNAs dictate the m6A activity of METTL3-METTL14.
source: These results suggests that: (a) the sequence and shape of the target RNAs dictate the m6A activity of METTL3-METTL14, and (b) that higher affinity substrates tend to show lower methylation levels, possibly due to slow off rates of m6A RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results comparing different RNA substrates.

claim: Higher affinity substrates tend to show lower methylation levels, possibly due to slow off rates of m6A RNA.
source: These results suggests that: (a) the sequence and shape of the target RNAs dictate the m6A activity of METTL3-METTL14, and (b) that higher affinity substrates tend to show lower methylation levels, possibly due to slow off rates of m6A RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and involves speculation about the mechanism.

claim: rNEAT2 inhibited the DNA methylation activity of METTL3-METTL14 with IC50 = 216 nM.
source: To further investigate RNA-mediated inhibition, we showed that the two structured RNAs (rTCE23 and rNEAT2) inhibited the DNA methylation activity of METTL3-METTL14 in a dose-dependent manner, with rNEAT2 (IC50 = 216 nM) showing 4-fold stronger inhibition than rTCE23 (IC50 = 887 nM) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by dose-dependent inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: rTCE23 inhibited the DNA methylation activity of METTL3-METTL14 with IC50 = 887 nM.
source: To further investigate RNA-mediated inhibition, we showed that the two structured RNAs (rTCE23 and rNEAT2) inhibited the DNA methylation activity of METTL3-METTL14 in a dose-dependent manner, with rNEAT2 (IC50 = 216 nM) showing 4-fold stronger inhibition than rTCE23 (IC50 = 887 nM) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by dose-dependent inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: rNEAT2 showed 4-fold stronger inhibition than rTCE23 of METTL3-METTL14 DNA methylation activity.
source: To further investigate RNA-mediated inhibition, we showed that the two structured RNAs (rTCE23 and rNEAT2) inhibited the DNA methylation activity of METTL3-METTL14 in a dose-dependent manner, with rNEAT2 (IC50 = 216 nM) showing 4-fold stronger inhibition than rTCE23 (IC50 = 887 nM) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by dose-dependent inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: An equimolar addition of rNEAT2 reduced the methyltransferase activity from 80.5% to 14.5%.
source: As shown in Figure 2f, an equimolar (with respect to d6T* DNA) addition of rNEAT2 or rTCE23 significantly reduced the methyltransferase activity from 80.5–14.5% to 7.3%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC/MS-based oligonucleotide intact mass analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: An equimolar addition of rTCE23 reduced the methyltransferase activity from 80.5% to 7.3%.
source: As shown in Figure 2f, an equimolar (with respect to d6T* DNA) addition of rNEAT2 or rTCE23 significantly reduced the methyltransferase activity from 80.5–14.5% to 7.3%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by LC/MS-based oligonucleotide intact mass analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Deoxyadenosine on d6T* and adenosine on rNEAT2 were the only modified bases in METTL3-METTL14 reactions.
source: We confirmed that deoxyadenosine on d6T* and adenosine on rNEAT2 were the only modified bases.
evidence: This is supported by nucleoside analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: In the absence of rNEAT2 or rTCE23, 86.3% of dAs on d6T* were modified.
source: In the absence of rNEAT2 or rTCE23, 86.3% of dAs on d6T* were modified.
evidence: This is supported by nucleoside analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: When rNEAT2 was present, only 14.4% of dAs on d6T* were modified.
source: When rNEAT2 or rTCE23 were present, only 14.4% and 7.4%, respectively, of dAs on d6T* were modified.
evidence: This is supported by nucleoside analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: When rTCE23 was present, only 7.4% of dAs on d6T* were modified.
